metadata.title: Effects of COVID-19 education policies on students’ learning proficiency in Latin America—Insights from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries and constructs student-level binary outcomes based on reaching Level 2 in math and reading. The analytic sample is restricted to schools closed due to the pandemic (including cases with missing closure days), and observations with missing ESCS are excluded (Costa Rica excluded entirely; remaining 10 countries kept after ESCS-missing removal). The manuscript reports both “weighted” and “unweighted” evaluation metrics for model performance, but it does not name the specific PISA weight variable(s) used in the ML training/evaluation. Because the paper applies ML classifiers (logit, neural networks, gradient boosted trees) and does not document a complex-survey weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedure, the exact survey-weight implementation cannot be verified from the provided text; the reported “weighted” metrics indicate some weighting was applied, but the variable name and replicate method are not specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Start from PISA 2022 student microdata for 11 LAC countries; exclude Costa Rica because ESCS is completely missing (6113 observations). Exclude remaining observations with missing ESCS in the other 10 countries, leaving 71,375 student observations. Keep key student/family covariates (Table 1) and merge with the school dataset containing COVID-19 policy variables (Tables 2–3). Restrict the working sample to schools closed due to the pandemic; the school-closure restriction yields 55,041 observations and 2,358 schools, with an additional note that this includes cases where the school closure variable is missing (7,259 student observations). Transform explanatory variables using one-hot encoding for categorical/binary inputs. Impute missing covariate values using KNN imputation (K=7) for the small proportion of missingness (55 covariates <5% missing; 13 covariates <10%). Construct binary outcomes for math and reading: compute mean achievement by averaging the 10 plausible values per subject, then apply PISA Level 2 thresholds (421 for math; 408 for reading) to define proficiency (Level 2 or above).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (age 15) Latin America—Math proficiency (Level 2+; binary from averaged PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (whole sample, weighted): Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost AUROC=0.8627, APRC=0.7261, ACC=0.8145, BACC=0.7503, F1=0.6474, MCC=0.5252. Unweighted: AUROC=0.8829, APRC=0.7707, ACC=0.8222, BACC=0.7713, F1=0.6846, MCC=0.5636. Best model is Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost; gaps vs NN and logit reported as smaller for weighted metrics (e.g., 1.7%–5.0% vs NN).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (age 15) Latin America the study leveraged CEP1: resources for students, CEP2: resources for teachers, CEP3: teacher communication, Number of days school closed, and Family SES (ESCS index) to predict Math proficiency (Level 2 or above), finding that Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost achieved the highest classification performance (e.g., weighted AUROC=0.8627) and that policy effects are non-linear with closure duration (CEP1 and CEP2 show positive associations in specific ranges, while CEP3 shows decreasing/negative tendencies at higher closure durations). This indicates that remote-learning policy packages should be designed with non-linear “duration-aware” intensity—especially prioritizing student resource support and teacher resources at medium-to-long closures—while avoiding assumptions of uniform benefits across time and groups.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (age 15) Latin America—Reading proficiency (Level 2+; binary from averaged PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (whole sample, weighted): Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost AUROC=0.8497, APRC=0.8586, ACC=0.7641, BACC=0.7644, F1=0.7685, MCC=0.5284. Unweighted: AUROC=0.8690, APRC=0.8692, ACC=0.7817, BACC=0.7817, F1=0.7837, MCC=0.5634. Best model is Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost; it is reported as superior to NN and logit across outcomes and sub-samples.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (age 15) Latin America the study leveraged CEP1: resources for students, CEP2: resources for teachers, CEP3: teacher communication, Number of days school closed, and Family support for education to predict Reading proficiency (Level 2 or above), finding that Gradient boosted trees/XGBoost achieved the best reading classification performance (e.g., weighted AUROC=0.8497) and that policy–achievement relationships are again non-linear with closure duration, with student resource support (CEP1) showing broader positive relative-probability patterns at longer closures. This indicates that reading recovery may be more responsive to student-facing learning resources during prolonged shutdowns, so policy emphasis on accessible materials (e.g., digital/text resources and structured learning) can be a practical lever for sustaining competency attainment.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Dominican Rep., Mexico, Panama, Peru, Paraguay, Uruguay), restricting the sample to schools closed due to COVID-19 and constructing binary outcomes for math and reading proficiency (Level 2+). Achievement is derived by averaging the 10 plausible values per subject and applying PISA Level 2 thresholds (421 math; 408 reading). Three ML classifiers are compared—logistic regression, neural networks, and gradient boosted trees (XGBoost)—with XGBoost selected as best-performing using AUROC during hyperparameter tuning and evaluated on a holdout set; for math (weighted) AUROC=0.8627 and for reading (weighted) AUROC=0.8497. The paper uses SHAP (TreeExplainer) to interpret non-linear and interaction effects of COVID-19 policy intensity (CEP1–CEP3) with closure duration and heterogeneity by gender and family SES. Results are correlational (no causal identification) and the manuscript does not fully document the exact PISA weight variable(s) used in the “weighted” ML evaluation, limiting precision of population-representativeness claims.
